title: SEMICON India Opens With Modi's Chip Push as EU Telecoms Battle a Huawei Ban and SpaceX Freezes Falcon 9 Orders
subhead: India kicks off its flagship semiconductor event as New Delhi doubles down on domestic chipmaking, while Europe's operators push back against a proposed Huawei/ZTE ban and a SpaceX launch-book freeze reshapes the commercial space market.

sections.heading: Semiconductor Geopolitics: SEMICON India Opens as New Delhi Doubles Down on Chips
sections.body:
Prime Minister Narendra Modi inaugurated the fifth edition of SEMICON India on September 17 at Yashobhoomi in New Delhi, under the theme 'Silicon to Systems: Building the Ecosystem,' according to ET CIO's coverage of the joint India Semiconductor Mission (ISM) and SEMI event. The three-day gathering, running to September 19, hosts over 500 exhibitors including 294 international companies and delegations from more than 40 countries, with 10 state-government pavilions.

The venue choice signals policy momentum. India has approved 12 projects under Semicon 1.0 and the Union Cabinet has approved Semicon 2.0 to speed the next phase, alongside design-tool support for 332 academic institutes and 105 startups and 24 startups cleared under the Design-Linked Incentive (DLI) scheme, per event materials. SEMI president and CEO Ajit Manocha framed India's goal as not merely joining the global supply chain but becoming integral to it.
sections.whyItMatters: SEMICON India has become the clearest marker of India's ambition to convert policy intent into manufacturing reality, entering the phase where global chipmakers test whether New Delhi's incentives translate into fabs that matter beyond assembly.

sections.heading: Telecoms & Network Sovereignty: Europe's Operators Push Back on Huawei/ZTE Ban
sections.body:
European telecom bosses warned on Tuesday against a proposed EU ban on equipment from high-risk vendors such as Huawei and ZTE, arguing it would raise investment costs, per an AFP report carried by ET Telecom. The Connect Europe lobby of operators signed an open letter from 17 top executives, including the CEOs of France's Orange, Germany's Deutsche Telekom and Spain's Telefonica, warning the Cybersecurity Act (CSA) under the Digital Networks Act risks draining capital needed for fibre, 5G and 6G.

The letter, which did not name China directly, said a blanket ban on non-EU suppliers would impose 'up to 40 billion euros ($46 billion) in replacement costs' on the sector. The proposal is being negotiated between the European Parliament and the 27 member states, after the Commission's 2023 call to exclude Huawei and ZTE produced insufficient results. The United States has long pressed allies to follow its lead in blocking Huawei gear.
sections.whyItMatters: The €40 billion price-tag debate puts a hard number on the cost of European network sovereignty, forcing a political choice between security doctrine and the capital operators says they need for the 5G-to-6G transition.

sections.heading: Space & Orbital Power: SpaceX Freezes New Falcon 9 Orders and China Sets a Sea-Launch Record
sections.body:
Italian launch firm Avio said on September 16 it is fielding an influx of commercial satellite operators after SpaceX suspended new commercial Falcon 9 reservations, according to SatNews. Avio CEO Giulio Ranzo said the manifest pinch follows SpaceX prioritising internal Starlink deployment, US Space Force national-security missions and NASA crewed flights, leaving commercial operators facing extended timelines.

The squeeze is pushing operators toward Avio's Vega C, Arianespace and Rocket Lab, with Avio expanding production at its Colleferro facilities in Italy. In the same 24-hour window, China's Gravity-1 Y3 rocket launched nine satellites in a sea-based mission off Shanghai, placing eight Qianfan (G60) constellation satellites and one EUHT test satellite into orbit at an 800-kilometer insertion altitude, per the Global Times and Science and Technology Daily. Orienspace's mission was the first sea-based mobile launch for a LEO broadband constellation, with a net payload exceeding three tonnes.
sections.whyItMatters: A Falcon 9 capacity crunch plus China's expanding sea-launch capability points to a two-sided rebalancing of launch supply — Western commercial demand finding alternatives while Beijing advances low-cost, mobile ways to build out its Qianfan internet constellation.

sections.heading: Critical Minerals: China's Refining Grip Still Holds as Demand Grows
sections.body:
A detailed analysis from Diálogo, carried by Eurasia Review on September 15, maps why Beijing's hold on critical minerals endures despite US investment. The IEA expects critical-mineral demand to rise more than 6 percent annually through 2030, and China accounts for roughly 90 percent of global rare-earth refining and separation capacity, according to supply-chain expert Eduardo Castellet Nogués of TRENDS Research & Advisory.

Latin America holds about half of the world's lithium and more than a third of its copper, with the Latin American Energy Organization (OLADE) putting the regional market near $180 billion. Yet the OECD says 62 percent of regional mineral exports still leave unprocessed, with Chinese state-backed firms dominant in the lithium triangle, Peru's copper belt and Brazil's lithium valley. Argentina's RIGI framework, Chile's critical-minerals strategy and Brazil's Mining Plan 2050 aim to keep more refining at home, but analysts describe them as a start rather than a match for China's processing lead.
sections.whyItMatters: Even as the US spends on domestic supply, the bottleneck sits in refining — where China retains decisive share — making processing capacity, not mining, the real fault line in the battery and clean-energy supply chain.

sections.heading: AI & Compute Sovereignty: Huawei's 3D Data Center and the Compute-Density Race
sections.body:
Huawei unveiled what it calls the world's first 3D data center, a vertically stacked four-layer architecture designed for increasingly dense AI clusters and gigawatt-scale infrastructure, according to Digitimes. The design targets the density wall hyperscalers are hitting as AI workloads demand ever-greater compute per square meter.

The announcement lands as Epoch AI scales its data center research to track 86 large AI facilities with 13.3 gigawatts of power and 13.9 million GPUs, covering roughly 46 percent of global AI compute, per Cryptobriefing. Chinese vendors competing under export-control headwinds are pushing system-level innovation — stacking, cooling and power design — rather than chasing raw GPU performance against US chipmakers.
sections.whyItMatters: As compute becomes the strategic input of the AI era, the competition is shifting from chips alone to the physical infrastructure — data center density, cooling and power — where Chinese vendors are trying to offset their silicon disadvantage.

sections.heading: Türkiye Angle: Global Chip and Launch Dynamics Frame Ankara's Options
sections.body:
No major Türkiye-specific tech-power announcement surfaced today, but the day's global developments frame Ankara's position. The EU Huawei/ZTE ban debate directly touches Turkish operators, who run significant Chinese-sourced radio gear and would face the same replacement-cost math Connect Europe quantifies for its own members if Brussels extends restrictions. Türkiye's 5G tender and its push for domestic equipment and defense-electronics production sit against the same backdrop of Huawei dependency and supply-chain security.

Meanwhile, the SpaceX Falcon 9 freeze and China's sea-launch capability matter for Turkey's emerging launch ambitions — a more crowded and costlier commercial market makes independent access to orbit more valuable, and Ankara's orbital plans come as both poles tighten their launch pipelines.
sections.whyItMatters: Ankara has a direct stake in both the EU's high-risk-vendor rules (given Huawei gear in Turkish networks) and the tightening global launch market, even though no domestic move drove today's headlines.

bottomLine: Today's tech-power picture is defined by infrastructure and access rather than a single shock. India used SEMICON to cast itself as the next serious chipmaking destination even as Europe confronted the true cost of removing Huawei gear from its networks, SpaceX's decision to freeze new commercial Falcon 9 launch bookings squeezed Western launch supply just as China demonstrated a new sea-launch route to its Qianfan constellation, and the critical-minerals analysis underlined that Beijing's refining dominance remains the stubborn bottleneck in the energy supply chain. The common thread is not who builds the best chip, but who controls the capacity — fabs, network gear, launch slots and refining — that everything else depends on, and today's headlines show both Washington's rivals and its allies maneuvering for position.
sources: ET Telecom (AFP), SatNews, Global Times / Science and Technology Daily, Eurasia Review (Diálogo), Digitimes, Cryptobriefing, ET CIO / India Semiconductor Mission
